intended_object: The "first non-singleton cell" target-cell selector from individualisation–refinement canonical labelling (McKay–Piperno / nauty). Given an ordered partition of {0,…,n−1}, it returns the start position of the first cell with more than one element, or none if the partition is discrete. This comes from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
This is executable code. It works on the library's array encoding of an ordered partition, `Part`, in nauty style: `cen[i]` is one past the last position of the cell containing position `i`. `cenTargetFrom cen n fuel i` walks from cell start to cell start (`i ↦ cen[i]`). It returns `some i` as soon as the current cell has size `cen[i] - i > 1`, and returns `none` once `i ≥ n` or the fuel runs out. Starting at position 0 with fuel `n` is enough, because a partition of n points has at most n cells. So on any well-formed partition the function returns exactly the start of the first non-singleton cell, or `none` when every cell is a singleton (the discrete partition). On malformed arrays the result is a junk value, but it still terminates.

The rule is the standard isomorphism-invariant target-cell selector from IR algorithms. There is no question of generality: the definition is tied to this particular data representation, so a broader setting does not apply. Mathlib has no counterpart, since it has no IR or ordered-partition canonical labelling machinery.

One could also call this an implementation detail of the algorithm and answer `not_a_mathematical_object`. I chose `faithful` because the docstring gives a precise specification and the code implements it correctly.
